content.p: On 24 January 2023, three children were strangled with exercise bands in the basement of their home in Duxbury, a coastal town south of Boston. Cora was 5, Dawson was 3 and Callan was 8 months old. Their mother, Lindsay Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, does not deny that she killed them. The question that has occupied courts for more than three years is why, and whether the law holds her responsible.

Clancy has not been convicted of anything. She pleaded not guilty to three counts of first-degree murder, relying on the Massachusetts insanity defence, which her lawyers describe as a plea that she lacked criminal responsibility. Her trial in Plymouth Superior Court ran for about five weeks in the summer of 2026. On 4 September a judge declared a mistrial after the jury said it could not reach a unanimous decision. The charges remain, and as of the last hearing reported, on 29 September 2026, prosecutors had not said whether they would try her again.

According to a timeline published by Marie Claire, Patrick Clancy, Lindsay's husband at the time, left the house that evening to collect takeout for the family. When he came back less than an hour later, the house was quiet and the bedroom door was locked. He found Lindsay lying in the back garden, barely conscious, with cuts to her wrists and neck, after she had jumped from a second-floor window. While paramedics treated her, he found the three children in the basement.

WCVB reported at the time that Patrick Clancy called 911 at about 6:10 p.m. District Attorney Timothy Cruz said Duxbury first responders found the children unconscious with obvious signs of trauma. Cora and Dawson were pronounced dead after being taken to Beth Israel Deaconess Hospital in Plymouth. Callan was flown to Boston Children's Hospital and was pronounced dead on 27 January.

Clancy was left paralysed from the waist down by the fall. She was treated at Brigham and Women's Hospital and has since been held at Tewksbury Hospital, a state facility. At an arraignment in early 2023, reported by Fox News, a judge set no monetary bail and allowed her treatment to continue. She faced charges of murder, strangulation, and assault and battery with a deadly weapon.

In a message on a fundraising page days after the deaths, Patrick Clancy wrote that he forgave his wife and asked others to do the same. He described her as someone who was "generously loving and caring". Authorities at that stage would not say whether mental illness had played any part.

Both sides in the trial agreed that Clancy was struggling in the months before the killings. At trial her mother and sister described a woman who grew anxious, paranoid and suicidal once her third child, Callan, was born. Her mother, Paula Musgrove, who often stayed at the Duxbury house to help with the children, said that at one point Clancy admitted to having thoughts of harming them. Susan Clancy, her former mother-in-law, described her as a loving and nurturing mother.

Medical records, as WBUR summarised them, showed that Clancy had been going to psychiatric clinicians and the emergency room, calling suicide hotlines, and had been admitted to an inpatient psychiatric hospital about three weeks before the killings. Her lawyers argued that she was overprescribed and took several medications, and that her care was disjointed. Prosecutors said she often did not take her psychiatric medications as prescribed and that most were low doses. Several of the clinicians who treated her testified for the prosecution that they never saw signs of psychosis.

The Associated Press reported that the killings happened less than three weeks after her discharge from that hospital stay. Patrick Clancy told the jury that after the birth of their third child she was under the care of several clinicians but continued to deteriorate. He said she had spoken of thoughts of harming herself and the children, but that he never thought she would hurt them. Both Lindsay and Patrick Clancy have since brought separate medical malpractice suits against some of her health care providers.

The trial attracted international attention and strong public feeling about maternal mental health. WBUR reported that proceedings were livestreamed, that crowds queued for seats, and that hundreds of supporters in pink shirts rallied outside the courthouse. Clancy did not testify. She attended in a wheelchair, with two nurses beside her, and wept several times. When a doctor described the children's injuries she sobbed loudly enough that the judge briefly paused proceedings, NPR reported. Jurors also heard two days of testimony from Patrick Clancy and played his 911 call.

The central legal question was narrower than the public debate. Under Massachusetts law, as WBUR explained, prosecutors must prove that a defendant's mental illness did not prevent her from appreciating that her act was wrong or from conforming to the law. Before deliberations, as the Boston Globe reported, Judge Sullivan planned to instruct jurors that the options for each child were first-degree murder, second-degree murder, manslaughter, or a finding of not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.

Reddington called 10 witnesses in under a week and rested on 21 August. His argument was that Clancy loved her children but lost her grip on reality because of bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis, a rare illness that researchers estimate affects one to two in 1,000 women after delivery, according to the AP.

Dr. Philip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist, told jurors that Clancy was severely depressed and had bipolar disorder that began after Callan's birth. He said she experienced "command hallucinations" telling her to kill the children and then herself, and that the psychotic break left her feeling removed from her body. Dr. Paul Zeizel, a forensic psychologist, testified that she had told him about a male voice ordering her to kill her children and herself. He said she had bipolar disorder with postpartum psychosis and had no appreciation of the wrongfulness of her act. Under questioning from prosecutors he accepted that she has not reported hearing voices since the killings.

Sheila Cavanaugh, a hospital chaplain who met Clancy after she was taken off a breathing tube, testified that Clancy first said, "I am so glad my children are safe," and later alluded to a persistent male voice that warned neither she nor the children would be safe if she disobeyed. Prosecutors pointed out that Cavanaugh's detailed notes never recorded a voice. Cavanaugh answered that chaplain notes are not verbatim transcripts and that she was not there to evaluate Clancy.

Prosecutors Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham argued that Clancy planned the killings, and the CBS station WFSB reported that they alleged she then faked a suicide attempt. In the Boston Globe's summary, they said she was depressed, overwhelmed and tired of her life, and decided to take the children with her because she did not trust anyone else to care for them. In her closing, Sprague argued that mental health policy was not on trial: "This case is not about our mental health system or how it treats women."

The prosecution's experts agreed that Clancy was mentally ill but not that she was psychotic. Dr. Kirk Heilbrun diagnosed bipolar II disorder, severe depression and dissociation. He told jurors that her intrusive thoughts were not auditory hallucinations, that it would be "very, very unusual" for someone with psychosis to hear a voice only once, and that a voice can offer "a convenient way of lessening your own culpability". The AP reported that a prosecution forensic psychologist concluded she killed the children because she wanted to end her own life but did not want to leave them behind. Under cross-examination Heilbrun agreed that it is better to examine someone sooner rather than later, since he interviewed her about three years after the killings.

Dr. Gregory Saathoff, a senior psychiatrist with the FBI's behavioural analysis unit, also diagnosed bipolar II. He called Clancy's claim that she heard the voice only during the 18 minutes of the killings highly unusual, and testified that Clancy retained the capacity to appreciate right from wrong. He described her conduct that day as "methodical and quite controlled": she took her daughter to a pediatrician, built a snowman with the children and texted photographs to her husband and mother. He said that after she missed a call from her husband she had "the presence of mind" to call back without disclosing what she was doing. Reddington noted that Saathoff interviewed Clancy only by video call, in May and June 2026, and that Resnick is a renowned expert on malingering. Saathoff said Resnick's opinion was that Clancy was not lying. Reddington also told a psychiatrist, Dr. Avram Mack, that Clancy showed nine of 10 symptoms of psychosis; Mack agreed that hearing voice commands would be a serious sign of it.

After closing arguments on 27 August, for which the judge allowed each side an hour, the jury began deliberating that afternoon. It sent the judge its first note of an impasse on Tuesday 1 September, and he told it to keep trying. By Thursday Reddington was citing two notes from the foreperson about one juror. He said that juror had admitted doubt but would not join the other 11 in finding Clancy not guilty. He asked the judge to remove the juror. Prosecutors objected and Sullivan refused, though he spoke to each juror privately and gave new instructions on reasonable doubt, saying it is not proof beyond all possible doubt.

On Friday 4 September, Reddington asked the Supreme Judicial Court for an emergency ruling to excuse or question the juror, writing that the juror's reasoning "reflects a bias against those who suffer from debilitating mental illness". He also asked the judge to poll the jury on lesser charges so that Clancy could not be retried for first-degree murder. The judge denied the poll, the court denied the emergency request, and the jury's final note said, "It is with a heavy heart that we report we are unable to come to a unanimous decision, and we will not be able to." Sullivan declared a mistrial.
Outlets differ on how long the jury had been out: NPR said six days; TNND said the mistrial came on the seventh day of deliberations.

Cruz said afterwards that the case "was, and has always been, about getting justice for those three little babies" and declined to say whether he would retry it. Reddington said the 11-1 split should make prosecutors reconsider. On 8 September he told Good Morning America that he was willing to listen to Cruz about a plea, according to Fox News, though earlier he had said prosecutors were not open to one. He also appealed to President Trump for a pardon; Fox News noted that a federal pardon cannot apply to a state prosecution. Patrick Clancy's lawyer, Howard Cooper, said the family had been the target of a "defamation campaign" built on baseless claims about Patrick's involvement in the children's deaths, and that law enforcement had been notified.

The juror who held out disputed the defence account through his own lawyer. In a statement reported by Fox, he said he "didn't have any doubts" and believed the evidence showed Clancy "knew exactly what she was doing and planned". Other jurors who spoke publicly said he appeared to acknowledge doubt but would not join the rest.

At the 29 September hearing, Reddington argued there had been a "total and complete lack of evidence" that Clancy killed the children, a position Buckingham called "laughable", noting that the defence had stipulated at trial to physical evidence establishing culpability. Buckingham said that "People can still have criminal responsibility despite a mental illness." Judge Sullivan took the defence motion for a not-guilty finding under advisement, as he did a prosecution request for a gag order on Reddington citing the "carnival atmosphere" of the first trial.

The next date is 2 November 2026, when the judge is to hear more defence motions, including one to dismiss the murder charges and one for a limited inquiry into the holdout juror, and to discuss a possible retrial date. Cruz told WBZ he had not decided whether to retry the case but was proceeding as if a second trial would happen. Reported options include a retrial, reduced charges or a plea; a retrial on second-degree murder would allow Clancy to waive a jury. If she is eventually found not criminally responsible, she would be committed to a state psychiatric facility under periodic court review.
